title: An online shop for a bookstore
metaTitle: A bookstore shop for browse and taste
excerpt: A bookstore shop should show browse, staff taste, and a way to ask. Build the book page around those, then keep checkout short instead of copying a marketplace.
alt: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band, deciding how a bookshop should present its shelves.
caption: A shared screen, the way a small shop decides what to show. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a bookstore website help someone do?
faqs.answer: It should help them browse, see what the staff would recommend, and ask a question about a specific book. Checkout should come after those are clear, and it should be short. A grid built like a large marketplace makes a small shop harder to understand.

faqs.question: How short should bookstore checkout be?
faqs.answer: Ask for the name, the address, a way to write to them, and payment. Show the shipping cost before they commit, and let them check out as a guest. An account can be offered after the order, for people who want a history.

faqs.question: Where should a bookseller's recommendation live?
faqs.answer: Put a short shelf on the site, with one sentence from a real person in the shop next to each book they chose. Keep the shelf small enough that the choice is visible. Rotate it when the table in the shop changes.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A bookstore ecommerce website has to feel like a shop with a point of view. The page should let someone browse, see what the staff would put in their hands, and ask a question. Checkout comes after that, and it should be short.

A marketplace grid fights those three jobs. It treats every title as a listing, every visitor as a stranger comparing sellers, and every question as a ticket. A bookshop is smaller than that. The site should be smaller than that too.

## Browse is the front of the shop

People come to a bookshop to look. They may have a title. They often do not. The site has to support both without turning the homepage into a search box on an empty page.

Browse needs a few doors, chosen by how a person actually looks:

- New books, with a date or a short note so "new" means something.
- A shelf the staff is willing to defend, named in plain language.
- Subjects you actually stock, not a department tree copied from a warehouse.
- A way back to search for the person who already knows the title.

Four doors is enough. Twelve doors means the shop has not decided what it is. If the range is wide, the doors can change with the month. They should still be few.

Search belongs on the page. It should not be the only path. A search-only shop tells people you have inventory and no taste. A bookshop without taste is a database. The web is already full of those.

Show covers at a size a person can read on a phone. The title and the author should sit with the cover, in type, because a thumbnail is not a promise. Price can sit there too. A shop can say the number on the shelf, not only on the book page.

## Staff taste is a shelf you can name

Taste is not a paragraph about loving books. Taste is a selection. Put it where a person can act on it.

A staff shelf works when each book has one sentence from a person in the shop. The sentence should say who it is for, or what it is like, in the voice the shop already uses at the counter. "If you liked the last novel we pressed on you, start here." That is a bookseller. A line that could sit on any jacket is not.

Keep the shelf short. Eight to sixteen books is a table. Eighty is a dump bin. The point of the shelf is that someone chose. If everything is recommended, nothing is.

Name the person when the shop is small enough that the name is true. A first name and a role is enough. Do not invent a committee. If two people buy for the shop, two notes are fine. If the founder writes them, say so.

Rotate the shelf when the table in the real shop rotates. A website that still recommends last spring's pile is describing a shop you no longer run. The page can say "on the table this week" and mean it.

Local presses, one author you always stock, a section for the city you are in: these are browse and taste at once. Give them a door if they are real. Leave them off the site if they are a wish. Write the sentences in the shop. The person who unpacked the carton will be shorter and truer than a paragraph drafted to sound literary.

## A way to ask

A bookshop gets questions a checkout form cannot answer. Do you have this in paperback. Can you order it. Is it the edition with the maps. Will you hold it until Saturday.

The site should make that ask easy to find, and specific. A contact page with a single email and no context is a closed door. A form that asks for an order number and a department is a help desk. The shop needs a question about a book.

Put the ask on the book page and on the homepage. The book page version should already know which book. The person should not have to paste a title you are already showing. Fields worth having: the question, a way to reply, and whether they want it held or ordered. Fields that can wait: an account, a password, a marketing checkbox.

Say when you answer. "We read these in the shop and reply the same day or the next morning" is a fact if it is true. If you only read them on certain days, say those days. A promise you cannot keep is worse than a slower true one.

Some questions are orders. "Please order this" can become a line in the cart if you stock special orders. Some questions are advice. Those should not be forced through checkout. Keep both paths, and put the shop hours next to the form so a person in town can still call.

## The book page

The product page is one book, not a listing template with the cover swapped. Build it in this order:

1. Cover, title, author, price.
2. Format: hardback, paperback, or whatever you actually sell. If you sell one format, say that once and do not show a dead selector.
3. One bookseller sentence, if this book is on the table. If it is not, do not write a fake one.
4. The facts a buyer uses: publisher, year, and whether it is in the shop now.
5. The ask, and the button to buy.

Publisher copy can sit lower. Many shops paste the whole jacket. A few lines are enough on the first screen. The person who wants the plot will scroll. The person who is deciding whether this is the book should not have to scroll to find the price.

In stock, low, or orderable. Use those words if they match how the shop works. "Available" is vague. A book in the back room and a book you will order from a distributor are different promises. Say which.

If you sell a small number of signed copies, that is a separate line with its own count. Do not hide it in a paragraph under the jacket copy. When the count hits zero, the line should leave. A signed-copy badge on a book you can no longer sign is a small lie, and book people notice.

Related books should be other books you chose, in small number. If you do not yet know what sits well beside this title, skip the row. A link back to the shelf is more honest than an automatic carousel.

Page titles should name the book. [Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) says each page needs a title that describes that page, and warns against boilerplate that makes every result look the same. A shop titled "Shop" on every book teaches no one which volume they will land on.

## A short checkout

Checkout is where bookshops copy the worst habits of large stores. Extra account creation. A coupon field before the total. Shipping described as calculated later, when you already know the rate for a single book in your own country.

[Baymard Institute](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) puts the average documented online cart abandonment rate at 70.22 percent, from 50 studies. In their reasons, 17 percent of US online shoppers have abandoned an order because checkout was too long or complicated, and 12 percent could not see or calculate the total cost up front. Their testing describes an ideal checkout as short as 12 to 14 form elements, against an average US checkout that shows 23.48 elements by default.

A book is a simple shipment. You can show the shipping cost, or a clear rule, before the person commits. Guest checkout should be the path. An account can be offered after the order, for people who want a history. It should not be the toll.

Ask for what the carrier needs. Name, address, a way to write to them if the book is delayed, payment. Skip the company name, the fax field, the survey about how they heard of you. If you sell gift wrap, one checkbox is enough. If you do not, leave the option out even when the theme included it.

The button should say what will happen. "Pay and we will pack this" is clearer than "Submit." Show the title in the summary so they can catch a wrong edition. Confirm the order on a page that can be reread, with the same facts, not only in an email.

Down the Cove, a public Hanabi project, was an ecommerce restructure, migration, and redesign. Borrow the refusal to let a template add steps a bookseller would never add at the counter.

## What a marketplace grid gets wrong

A grid of equal tiles, filters for every attribute, star ratings, and a seller name is a reasonable shape for a place with a huge range. It is a poor shape for a room with tables.

Filters help when the catalog is large and the attributes are real: format, language, subject, in the shop today. Filters are noise when they exist because the theme had slots. A shop with a few hundred books needs the doors from the front of the shop and a search box that works. It does not need five facets and a sort menu with eight strategies.

Ratings from strangers are not your taste. If you do not have a review practice you stand behind, leave the stars off. A bookseller sentence does more work, and it does not pretend the shop is a poll.

Sponsored positions, badges you did not earn, and countdown timers are furniture from another kind of store. They make a small shop look like it is pretending. Take them out of the theme even if the switch is buried in a setting named "boost conversion."

The grid can still exist as a way to scan covers. Keep the crop consistent so the scan feels like one shop. Mixed crops, some with margins and some bleeding off the tile, look unfinished. That problem is mostly photographic.

The pictures have to carry browse and the staff's taste, which is why the next piece is [product photography for a bookstore](/blog/product-photography-for-a-bookstore).

If you want those pages scoped with someone who will also build them, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min).

## What to hand over before design

A studio can design this shop faster when the bookseller arrives with the decisions already named. The visual work then has somewhere to go.

Bring the doors in the order you would walk a new customer through the real shop. Bring a short stack of covers that represent the range. Bring three bookseller sentences you are proud of, and one question from last week that the site cannot answer. Bring the shipping rule in one line, including the awkward case, such as a heavy art book.

Say what you will not do. If you will not run reviews or same-day delivery, write that down. The template will offer both unless someone refuses. The build can stay a catalog, a book page, an ask, and a short checkout. A loyalty program and a blog you will not write are how a simple shop becomes a theme demo.
